title: Doubly robust inference via calibration
problem: Doubly robust estimators of linear functionals of a regression function (e.g. average treatment effects) are consistent if either nuisance function is consistent, but asymptotic normality and valid confidence intervals typically require both nuisances to converge fast enough. Can inference be made doubly robust as well — asymptotically normal when only one nuisance is well estimated and the other converges arbitrarily slowly or is inconsistent?
setting: Semiparametric estimation of linear functionals of the outcome regression (a subclass of mixed-bias parameters), with black-box / machine-learning nuisance estimators. Cross-fitting is used. Two nuisances: the outcome regression and the Riesz representer of the functional. Asymptotics: n to infinity, learner-agnostic rates; the key structural assumption is an asymptotic partial orthogonality condition. Evaluated on semi-synthetic benchmark datasets.
method: Calibrated debiased machine learning (calibrated DML): standard cross-fitted DML is augmented by calibrating each cross-fitted nuisance estimate with an isotonic regression adjustment, so the calibrated nuisances satisfy a set of calibration score equations. Under partial orthogonality this makes the one-step / DML estimator asymptotically normal when either the regression function or the Riesz representer is estimated at a sufficient rate, regardless of the other. A bootstrap-assisted procedure builds confidence intervals without estimating further nuisances.
contribution: Shows that calibrating the nuisance estimators inside a doubly robust procedure upgrades double robustness of consistency to double robustness of asymptotic normality: under an asymptotic partial orthogonality condition the calibrated DML estimator is root-n normal if either nuisance is estimated well enough, the other being allowed to be inconsistent. Provides an isotonic-regression implementation (a few lines added to existing DML pipelines), a bootstrap for confidence intervals, and an affirmative answer to a standing open question on learner-agnostic doubly robust inference.

mathematical_objects.name: doubly robust estimator
mathematical_objects.role: The estimation framework whose inferential (not just point-estimation) robustness is the target; the paper turns double robustness of consistency into double robustness of asymptotic normality.

mathematical_objects.name: Neyman orthogonality
mathematical_objects.role: The relaxation that drives the result: only an asymptotic partial orthogonality condition (weaker than full second-order orthogonality) is required for the calibrated estimator to be doubly robust for inference.

mathematical_objects.name: Riesz representer
mathematical_objects.role: One of the two nuisance functions; the linear functional is represented as an inner product against it, and calibrating it is one half of the calibration step.

mathematical_objects.name: isotonic regression
mathematical_objects.role: The concrete calibration operator applied to cross-fitted nuisance predictions; a step-function fit that enforces the calibration score equations.

mathematical_objects.name: calibration
mathematical_objects.role: The property required of the nuisance estimators; satisfying the calibration score equations is exactly what the doubly robust asymptotic-normality argument relies on.

mathematical_objects.name: cross-fitting
mathematical_objects.role: Decouples nuisance estimation error from the empirical process term so black-box learners can be used; calibration is applied fold-wise to the cross-fitted estimates.

mathematical_objects.name: bootstrap
mathematical_objects.role: Constructs confidence intervals for the calibrated DML estimator without additional nuisance estimation.

limitations: Requires an asymptotic partial orthogonality condition; the extracted text does not spell out how restrictive this is or how to check it in practice, and it is the load-bearing assumption.
Confined to linear functionals of the outcome regression; extension to the full mixed-bias class is only sketched in an appendix and left to future work.
Isotonic calibration and TMLE targeting enforce incompatible score equations, so a calibrated estimator with the plug-in property is not yet available.
Empirical evidence is semi-synthetic benchmarks only; no real-data study and no adversarial stress test of the 'one nuisance inconsistent' regime.
Intro section was not in the extract; the precise estimand definitions, rate conditions, and the statement of the partial orthogonality condition were read only through the abstract and conclusion.
The slowly-converging nuisance still needs to satisfy calibration; 'arbitrarily slow' convergence is conditional on that, which is a real constraint on the black-box learner.
open_questions: How verifiable or plausible is asymptotic partial orthogonality in standard causal setups (ATE under unconfoundedness, policy value, incremental effects)?
Can a single procedure reconcile isotonic calibration with TMLE targeting so the estimator is simultaneously plug-in and doubly robust for inference?
Does the framework extend to sequential / longitudinal parameters with multiple and sequential robustness?
What is the finite-sample cost of the extra isotonic step when both nuisances are already well estimated — is there a coverage/efficiency tradeoff?
cross_domain_note: Squarely statistics (semiparametric causal inference). The isotonic-regression and calibration machinery connects to shape-constrained estimation; the Riesz-representer framing connects to functional-analytic representation results.

title: Parameter Estimation for Time-Scaled Inhomogeneous Phase-Type Distributions from Discrete Observations
problem: How can one estimate the parameters of a time-scaled inhomogeneous phase-type (IPH) distribution when the underlying multi-state process is observed only at discrete, irregularly spaced time points, so that transition times and the absorption time are latent and estimation is a missing-data problem?
setting: Continuous-time finite-state inhomogeneous Markov jump process whose sub-intensity matrix has the time-scaled form Lambda(t) = h_beta(t) Lambda, so the process maps to a homogeneous Markov jump process under a deterministic time change. Panel / multi-state data: only the state at discrete irregular observation times is recorded; exact jump and absorption times are unobserved. Parametric families studied are matrix-Gompertz and matrix-Weibull. Frequentist likelihood-based inference; simulation plus a coronary allograft vasculopathy (CAV) progression application.
method: A Stochastic EM algorithm with Markov-bridge data augmentation. Each iteration: (simulation) simulate the latent continuous-time trajectory conditional on the observed discrete states using Markov-bridge sampling on the time-transformed homogeneous process; (maximization) update the baseline sub-intensity matrix Lambda by its closed-form complete-data maximum-likelihood estimator, and refine the time-scaling parameter beta by gradient ascent on the same complete-data log-likelihood. Reported estimates come from complete-data MLE updates, avoiding constrained nonlinear optimization of the observed-data likelihood.
contribution: Gives the first inference procedure for time-scaled IPH distributions under discrete, irregular observation of the latent jump process, combining Markov-bridge data augmentation with Stochastic EM so that every parameter update is a closed-form or gradient complete-data MLE step. Establishes identifiability conditions separating the baseline sub-intensity matrix from the time-scaling function, and validates on matrix-Gompertz / matrix-Weibull simulations and CAV progression data with a homogeneous-model comparison.

mathematical_objects.name: phase-type distribution
mathematical_objects.role: The model class being fitted: the absorption-time law of a finite-state Markov jump process, here in its time-inhomogeneous, time-scaled subclass, used to capture heavy tails and non-constant hazards.

mathematical_objects.name: Markov jump process
mathematical_objects.role: The latent continuous-time process whose sub-intensity matrix carries the parameters; its discrete-time observation is what makes estimation a missing-data problem.

mathematical_objects.name: time change
mathematical_objects.role: Structural device: h_beta(t) integrated gives a deterministic clock change mapping the inhomogeneous process to a homogeneous MJP, which forces the intensity matrices to commute and makes transition probabilities and bridge simulation tractable.

mathematical_objects.name: stochastic EM algorithm
mathematical_objects.role: The estimation engine: replaces the intractable conditional expectation of the complete-data score with a simulated complete path, then maximizes.

mathematical_objects.name: Markov bridge
mathematical_objects.role: Data-augmentation mechanism: samples latent trajectories of the jump process conditioned on matching the observed states at the discrete observation times.

mathematical_objects.name: maximum likelihood estimation
mathematical_objects.role: Provides the closed-form maximization update for the baseline sub-intensity matrix and the objective whose gradient updates the time-scaling parameter.

mathematical_objects.name: identifiability
mathematical_objects.role: Object of a theoretical result: conditions under which the baseline sub-intensity matrix and the time-scaling function can be separately recovered.

limitations: Restricted to the time-scaled subclass Lambda(t) = h_beta(t) Lambda; general IPH models where intensity matrices do not commute are explicitly out of reach of this approach.
Stochastic EM gives no exact standard errors from the algorithm itself; the extracted text does not state how uncertainty is quantified (observed information, bootstrap, or Louis-type identity).
No conclusion section and no methods section were available; convergence properties of the SEM iteration, Monte Carlo sample-size choices, and mixing of the Markov-bridge sampler are not visible.
Consistency / asymptotic normality of the resulting estimator is asserted only implicitly via 'complete-data MLE'; the extracted text does not present a formal large-sample theorem.
Empirical validation is one medical dataset (CAV) plus simulations from two parametric families; robustness to misspecification of h_beta is not discussed in the extracted text.
Identifiability is claimed but the conditions themselves are not stated in the available sections, so their practical bite is unclear.
open_questions: What are the asymptotic properties (rate, limiting distribution) of the SEM estimator as the number of subjects grows with a fixed discrete observation grid?
How does estimation degrade as the observation grid coarsens relative to the process's jump rate?
Can the Markov-bridge + SEM scheme be extended to piecewise-constant or non-commuting inhomogeneous intensities without losing the closed-form maximization step?
How sensitive are estimates to the parametric choice of the scaling function h_beta, and is there a diagnostic for its misspecification?
cross_domain_note: The IPH / Markov-jump-process machinery is shared with probability, but the contribution here is an estimator and its identifiability, so it sits in statistics. A probability curator interested in endpoint-conditioned jump processes / bridge simulation for their own sake could also card it.

title: A Two Stage Quasi-Likelihood Estimation Method for High Dimensional Generalized Structural Equation Models
problem: Estimating high-dimensional generalized structural equation models (equivalently generalized linear latent variable models) is computationally hard: the observed-data likelihood is a p-dimensional integral over the latent space, full-information maximum likelihood is intractable for discrete indicators, and there is no practical algorithm for outcome families such as Poisson, negative binomial, or gamma. How can the structural regression coefficients be estimated at scale, stably, for arbitrary GLM outcome families?
setting: n independent subjects; a p-vector of latent predictors eta ~ N(0, Phi) measured by a J-vector of mixed binary/ordinal/continuous indicators through a linear factor measurement model Z = nu + Lambda eta + epsilon; an outcome y whose conditional mean given eta follows a GLM (or quasi-likelihood family) with link g and structural coefficient vector beta. High-dimensional latent space is the regime of interest. Frequentist estimation; evaluation by Monte Carlo simulation plus a Big Five Inventory application with ordinal indicators. No asymptotic theory presented in the available sections.
method: Two-Stage Quasi-Likelihood EM (TSQLEM), a limited-information estimator that separates the measurement model from the structural model. Stage 1 approximates the conditional distribution of the latent variables given the observed indicators, eta | Z. Stage 2 derives the conditional first and second moments of the outcome given the indicators, y | Z, either in closed form or by Monte Carlo integration, and plugs them into marginal quasi-score estimating equations for the structural parameters, solved by iteratively reweighted least squares. The full joint likelihood is never evaluated.
contribution: Introduces the TSQLEM framework: by decoupling the measurement model from the structural model and estimating the structural coefficients from marginal quasi-score equations built on conditional moments of y | Z, it makes high-dimensional GSEM estimation numerically stable and fast, and extends tractable estimation to quasi-likelihood outcome families (Poisson, negative binomial, gamma) that lack existing algorithms. Simulations report large runtime reductions and lower MSE / structural bias relative to full- and limited-information competitors.

mathematical_objects.name: generalized linear latent variable model
aliases: confirmatory factor model with GLM outcome
mathematical_objects.role: The model class being estimated: a latent Gaussian factor measurement model coupled to a GLM structural equation linking latent predictors to an outcome.

mathematical_objects.name: quasi-likelihood
mathematical_objects.role: Basis of the structural-stage estimator: only conditional mean and variance are specified, so the method accommodates Poisson, negative binomial, gamma and other families with no tractable full likelihood.

mathematical_objects.name: expectation-maximization algorithm
mathematical_objects.role: Overall iterative scaffold: alternates recovering the conditional latent distribution (stage 1) with updating structural parameters (stage 2).

mathematical_objects.name: iteratively reweighted least squares
mathematical_objects.role: Numerical scheme that solves the approximate quasi-score equations for the structural coefficients at each iteration.

mathematical_objects.name: conditional moments
aliases: conditional expectation and variance of y given Z
mathematical_objects.role: The estimating equations are built from E[y | Z] and Var[y | Z]; deriving these exactly or by simulation is the technical core of stage 2.

mathematical_objects.name: Monte Carlo integration
mathematical_objects.role: Evaluates the conditional moments / latent-space integral when no closed form exists, replacing exponential-in-p Gauss-Hermite quadrature.

mathematical_objects.name: limited-information estimation
mathematical_objects.role: Design principle: isolating the measurement model from the structural model to cut cost and to blunt interpretational confounding, in which a local measurement misspecification biases structural parameters under joint fitting.

limitations: No methods or conclusion section was available; the exact stage-1 approximation of eta | Z, the form of the quasi-score equations, and the treatment of the factor loadings/thresholds are not visible.

No theoretical properties are stated in the extracted text — no consistency, no asymptotic variance, no standard-error construction for the two-stage estimator (a known difficulty for sequential estimators, where stage-1 uncertainty must propagate).

Two-stage / limited-information estimators are generally less efficient than FIML when the model is correctly specified; the extracted text frames this only as a robustness benefit and does not quantify the efficiency loss.
Stage 1 relies on a Gaussian latent structure and a linear factor measurement model; robustness to non-normal latent variables or nonlinear measurement is not discussed.

'High-dimensional' refers to the latent dimension p; there is no explicit sparsity or regularization on Phi, Lambda, or beta in the available text, so the high-dimensional regime's statistical (as opposed to computational) challenges are unaddressed.
Empirical validation is simulations plus one psychometric dataset (Big Five); generalization across indicator types and outcome families is asserted, not demonstrated in the extract.
open_questions: What are the large-sample properties of the TSQLEM estimator, and how is stage-1 estimation uncertainty propagated into structural standard errors?
How much efficiency is sacrificed relative to FIML / MHRM under correct specification, as a function of p and indicator type?
Does the Monte Carlo integration in stage 2 introduce bias or variance that needs its own control (sample-size schedule, variance reduction)?
Can the two-stage split be combined with regularization on the loading matrix to handle genuinely high-dimensional indicator sets?
cross_domain_note: Statistics (latent variable modeling / estimation). Arrives in psychometric clothing (SEM, Big Five) but the estimator is family-agnostic and separable from the application, so it clears the charter's transferability test; tag as [applied-field-methodology].
